claims.text: An integrated DFT-BTE-GK framework will predict the lattice thermal conductivity of defect-free HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than earlier analytical models.
The integrated framework can decouple lattice thermal conductivity from the electronic contribution.
Below 200 K, the framework will improve prediction accuracy by at least approximately 20% relative to earlier analytical models.
The intended material is bulk crystalline HfNbTaTiZr with minimal defects and oxygen contamination.
The framework separately computes lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity.
The proposed applicability range is approximately 150–1200 K.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are comparable below 200 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT-derived lattice and electronic structures provide the basis for resolving phonon dispersion and coupling.
DFT and BTE calculate phonon properties, while Green–Kubo relations calculate phonon lifetimes or correlation functions.
Computing phonon transport independently of electronic transport isolates the lattice contribution and improves precision.
Predicted low-temperature lattice thermal conductivity will deviate by less than ±20% from experimentally isolated lattice conductivity.
Older analytical models deviate by 30–50% from experimental data.
Earlier analytical models commonly provide combined total-conductivity estimates that conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
The hypothesis may not apply to HfNbTaTiZr samples containing significant oxygen contamination, exemplified as more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
The framework is expected to remain accurate up to 1200 K.
Above 1200 K, anharmonicity and additional scattering mechanisms could reduce the framework's accuracy.
The estimated accuracy improvement may vary by ±5%.
Below 150 K, electron–phonon coupling may make complete separation of electronic and lattice transport more uncertain.
Inelastic neutron scattering or isotope-substitution methods can be used to help isolate the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution.

The hypothesis is falsified if predicted lattice conductivity differs by more than ±25% from the experimentally isolated contribution across the tested regime, or if transport decoupling cannot be experimentally verified.
